newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, Palestinians to meet again after setback.
newsitem.headline: Israel, Palestinians to meet again after setback.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian negotiators plan to meet again later on Friday after a setback in their push to strike a deal on the long-delayed Israeli troop pullback from the West Bank town of Hebron.
The two sides ended a meeting early on Friday because of deep differences among members of the Israeli delegation, PLO officials told reporters.

Palestinian delegates looked angry as they left the meeting but Israeli spokesman Moshe Fogel said progress had been made and that U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross and the Palestinian and Israeli delegations would meet again at 9.a.m. (0700 GMT).
"I think that significant progress has been made tonight," said Fogel.
Ross said: "They have narrowed the differences. They're working hard but there are still differences to be overcome."
Only hours before the meeting broke up, the Israelis and Palestinians had said they were close to a deal on an Israeli troop withdrawal from Hebron.
Palestinian officials said they spent hours waiting for the Israeli delegation to settle an internal dispute over issues that should have been agreed and drafted over the troop redeployment.

"We came to Eilat with an agreement to start drafting a protocol on a Hebron deal after the major issues were resolved earlier," said a PLO (Palestine Liberation Organisation) official, who asked not to be identified.
"However, internal disputes of the Israeli delegation prevented any progress. They wanted the meetings to be postponed until next week."
Palestinian officials said the differences were between the politicians and military representatives in the Israeli delegation.
The Palestinians said they expected the Israelis to resolve their differences and return to the talks with a greater readiness to conclude the agreement.
Earlier, both sides had voiced optimism about striking a deal within hours.

"The issues have been resolved," one Palestinian official said as the marathon talks went into Friday. "If there are no problems in the drafting, within 24 hours there will be positive results and an agreement."
The Palestinians even said it could be signed on Friday or Sunday and start coming into force 10 days later.
Israeli and Palestinian negotiators met in Eilat in Israel and Taba in Egypt, neighbouring Red Sea resorts, to hammer out issues and a protocol for implementing the pullback.
"Within hours the matter could be completed," Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy told Israel's Channel Two on Thursday.

Israel has held up redeployment in Hebron, citing security concerns for the 400 Jews who live and study in enclaves among 100,000 Arabs. The city is sacred to Moslems and Jews as the burial place of the biblical Abraham.
The redeployment, due to have taken place in March, was delayed by Islamic suicide bombings in Israel and later put off by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu elected in May.
Palestinians view the Hebron redeployment -- part of a 1995 deal with the previous left-centre Israeli government -- as a litmus test of Netanyahu's commitment to peace.
Late on Thursday night the main talks moved to a hotel in Eilat -- away from the scrutiny of journalists who had assembled in Taba for talks earlier in the day.

A Palestinian official said major stumbling blocks were removed during a meeting on Thursday between Israeli army chief Amnon Shahak, PLO negotiator Abu Mazen, Palestinian Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbu and Ross.
Palestinian officials said Israel was no longer insisting on establishing a buffer zone or on the right to hot pursuit of wanted Palestinians in areas of Hebron coming under PLO control.
They said it was also agreed that talks on all other outstanding issues in a 1995 interim deal would start immediately after the Hebron agreement was concluded.

These issues would include further redeployments, the release of Palestinian prisoners, safe passage between the West Bank and Gaza Strip, operation of a Gaza airport for Palestinians and allowing more Palestinians to work in Israel.
Also on Thursday, Netanyahu's office declined comment on an Israeli television report that a secret message from Syria could enable their long-stalled peace talks to resume.

A spokeswoman would not comment on the Channel Two report that Netanyahu's political adviser Dore Gold secretly met U.S. diplomat Edward Djerejian who was returning from a meeting with Syrian President Hafez al-Assad in Damascus.
It said they met at the Allenby Bridge connecting the West Bank to Jordan.
Netanyahu insists he is keen to make peace but Arabs are sceptical because he opposes swapping occupied land for peace -- a foundation of the talks launched in Madrid in 1991.
Syria demands the return of all of the Golan Heights captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war. Netanyahu opposes giving up any of the strategic plateau.
